newsitem.title: USA: Dole hits ethics, Clinton appeals to young voters.
newsitem.headline: Dole hits ethics, Clinton appeals to young voters.

text.p: President Bill Clinton stormed through the South on Friday, trying to steal Republican territory from his frustrated challenger Bob Dole, who denounced the media and angrily scolded voters to wake up to Clinton's alleged ethical lapses.

Dole and independent candidate Ross Perot have both blasted Clinton and the Democratic Party in recent days for taking questionable campaign contributions from foreign interests and a convicted drug dealer.

Clinton, stressing family values issues in the closing days of the presidential race and ignoring Dole's attacks, used an outdoor rally in Georgia, the home state of House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, to unveil a plan to let 100,000 college students teach children to read.

Making a direct appeal to younger voters, Clinton said, "This is your election and we need you. You have most of your tomorrows in front of you. You have your future out there ahead of you, and you have to decide that."
While in Atlanta, Clinton also spoke by telephone with hundreds of black ministers in 32 states, urging them to get their followers to the voting booth on Nov. 5.
In Texas, Dole unleashed a scathing attack on Clinton and the national news media.
Dole's speech was a litany of what he said were ethical violations by the Clinton administration, coupled with an angry condemnation of the "liberal media" and voters for failing to pay attention.

Dole also asked Reform Party candidate Ross Perot to endorse his candidacy if he did not want Clinton to be re-elected -- his first public comments since his campaign's unsuccessful bid this week to persuade Perot to quit the race.

In a stinging speech, an agitated Dole slammed Clinton for refusing to say he would not pardon individuals connected to Whitewater, saying the president was "sending a signal" to defendants to sit tight until after the election.
He also tried to tie the president to the controversy over improper White House gathering of Republican FBI files.
"Where is the outrage in America? Where is the outrage in America? Where has the media gone in America?" Dole thundered at a rally in Houston.

"We have the president of the United States sitting down there with 900 FBI files, one might be one of yours ... And then we have the president of the United States who won't say he won't pardon somebody who did business with him and might implicate him later on. Where is the outrage in America?"

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, traveling with Clinton in Georgia, responded, "Bob Dole went negative on Bill Clinton and that didn't work. Now Bob Dole has gone negative on America, and that's not going to work either."
A series of national polls released on Friday showed Clinton solidifying his lead over Dole as the election drew nearer.
The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Dole lost ground on Thursday following the disclosure that his campaign manager made an abortive appeal to Perot to drop out of the campaign.

With Election Day 11 days away, Clinton led Dole by 11 percentage points, up from 8.7 points the day before. An ABC poll put Clinton's lead at 12 points and noted Perot's support had inched up to 8 percent. A CNN/USA Today/Gallup poll showed Clinton leading Dole by 17 points and gave Perot 8 percent.

A poll of 46,509 college students conducted Oct. 23 by Follett College Stores at its 500 U.S. college bookstores showed Clinton leading with 61.3 percent of the vote, compared to just 27.1 percent for Dole, and 7.1 percent for Perot.

Meanwhile Dole's campaign disclosed figures suggesting it would be heavily outspent by Clinton between now and the election on Nov. 5. According to the latest monthly reports filed with the Federal Election Commission, the Clinton campaign had $25.1 million left to spend as of Oct. 16, while the Dole campaign had $13.3 million.
